\chapter{Good Morning}
\label{ch:ka-good-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{29}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish someone good morning in Kannada and judge when it will sound too formal.}

Say \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} — śubha + udaya, \textquotedblleft{}auspicious rising\textquotedblright{} — and note the formal/written skew that makes \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ} the safer casual morning greeting.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[śubhōdaya]{\kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} (śubhōdaya) — \textquotedblleft{}good morning,\textquotedblright{} a third root for morning}

\label{lesson:KA-C29-shubhodaya}



\begin{quote}
You already have \kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}, the everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{} This greeting reaches for a completely different word for the same idea — and, honestly, this lesson's twist is about how uncertain its own \textquotedblleft{}everyday\textquotedblright{} status turns out to be, once you look closely.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ}} (\textbf{śubhōdaya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good morning}\textquotedblright{} — is built from \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ}} (\emph{śubha}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good, auspicious}\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\kn{ಉದಯ}} (\emph{udaya}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rising, sunrise},\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \textbf{ud-} \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{i} \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} — the same root behind \textbf{\kn{ಸೂರ್ಯೋದಯ}}, \emph{sūryōdaya}, \textquotedblleft{}sunrise\textquotedblright{} itself). This is a \textbf{completely different word} from \textbf{\kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}} (\emph{beḷagge}, Chapter 26's native \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) — Kannada now has (at least) two unrelated roots circling the idea of morning: one native (\textquotedblleft{}the shining\textquotedblright{}), one Sanskrit (\textquotedblleft{}the rising\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's where this lesson needs real care. Some sources describe \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ}} as the most common everyday way to say \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} in Kannada — but these are largely the same genre of generic phrasebook site whose claims about Hindi's \dv{सुप्रभात} turned out, on closer inspection, to be overstated. A more careful source instead describes \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} as reserved mainly for \textbf{formal or written} contexts — speeches, greeting cards, WhatsApp images — calling it \textquotedblleft{}not as frequently used in daily conversations\textquotedblright{} as \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}}/\textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ತೆ}}, and at least one native-speaker account suggests casual spoken Kannada often reaches for \textbf{English} \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} instead of \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} entirely. Taken together, this looks like the \textbf{same} formal/written skew already found for Hindi's \dv{सुप्रभात}, not the genuine cross-language contrast a first pass at the sources might suggest. A native alternate, \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಮುಂಜಾನೆ}} (\emph{śubha muñjāne}, using \emph{muñjāne}, \textquotedblleft{}the early morning, before sunrise\textquotedblright{}), also exists as a real, attested greeting construction — but its own register isn't independently confirmed here either.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śubhōdaya\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good morning,\textquotedblright{} śubha + udaya
  \item the root contrast — beḷagge is native \textquotedblleft{}shining\textquotedblright{}; udaya is Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}rising\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest note — sources conflict, but the more careful ones point to the same formal/written skew already found for Hindi
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} share a root with \kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}? (\textbf{No} — \kn{ಉದಯ}, \textquotedblleft{}rising,\textquotedblright{} is a completely different Sanskrit root from native \kn{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}'s \textquotedblleft{}shining.\textquotedblright{}) Is \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} genuinely common in everyday casual Kannada speech? (\textbf{Unclear, and possibly not} — sources conflict; the more careful ones describe it skewing formal/written, with \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}/\kn{ನಮಸ್ತೆ} covering casual mornings instead, and one native-speaker account suggests English \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} often gets used in casual speech instead of \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ} entirely.)
\end{tcolorbox}
